name: Amuzgo
packetScope: Three substantive new historical/community works, primarily on Xochistlahuaca in Guerrero; one renewed short community self-description outside the count. No Site/canonical changes.

sources.title: Experiencias en torno a la enseñanza, aprendizaje y difusión de la lengua ñomndaa del estado de Guerrero
sources.author: Bartolomé López Guzmán
sources.publisher: El Colegio de Guerrero and Editora Laguna, in De la oralidad a la palabra escrita; reading copy hosted by UNAM Biblioteca Jurídica Virtual
sources.annotation: López Guzmán explicitly writes as a member of the Nn’anncue Ñomndaa people. His account follows teachers, parents, a civil association and school projects. Its participant perspective and criticisms remain attributed; it is not a current independent evaluation or a history of all Amuzgo communities.
sources.contentReviewScope: Selected actual chapter pages 231–238 (PDF pages 1–8 of 26), especially first-person positioning, teacher formation, 1997 association and El Porvenir projects. Separate volume title/imprint/contents PDF inspected.

sources.title: No morirá la flor de la palabra… La radio comunitaria indígena en Guerrero y Oaxaca
sources.author: Giovanna Gasparello
sources.publisher: Nueva Antropología / Asociación Nueva Antropología A.C.; SciELO reading copy
sources.annotation: Selected passages give substantial Radio Ñomndaa evidence within a comparative study. They include reported community roles and participants' perspectives. Observations date to the research period; other stations' experiences and the author's legal/political arguments cannot be silently assigned to every Amuzgo community.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual article opening page133 and selected pages143–148 (PDF1 and11–16 of22), especially Radio Ñomndaa's organization, recording activity and attributed intercultural discussion. No full-article claim.

sources.title: Del silencio a la palabra. La experiencia de las lideresas indígenas de Xochistlahuaca, Guerrero
sources.author: Irma Guadalupe Aguirre Pérez
sources.annotation: Aguirre Pérez uses interviews and life histories to examine different routes into leadership. It contributes women's experiences and generational differences. Her structural and political judgments are interpretations from a dated local study, not timeless rules or a present assessment of named people or all Amuzgo institutions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual selected article text: introduction page101, methods pages105–106, barriers and leadership/mobility passages109–113, comparison114–115. Publisher metadata and CC BY4.0 licence checked; original PDF routes failed, actual full-text reading copy supplied passages.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Teachers and parents building community institutions
claimBlocks.text: Writing as an Nn’anncue Ñomndaa participant, Bartolomé López Guzmán recalls teachers questioning schooling that devalued their language and identity. He describes courses, collaboration with parents, and the creation of a sociocultural association in 1997. His account follows particular El Porvenir school projects in Xochistlahuaca, where teachers developed locally grounded approaches. This is an organizing history with setbacks and differing responses, rather than evidence that one curriculum reached every Amuzgo school or continues unchanged today.

In her 2012 study, Gasparello describes Radio Ñomndaa as more than a transmitter. Community representatives connected the project with local needs, while recording activity supported musicians and preserved material for later listeners. The account also acknowledges political divisions and an unfinished effort to build dialogue. These observations concern a particular project and research period; they do not establish unanimous support, present programming, or the same organization in Oaxaca's Amuzgo communities.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed pages143–148; organization on146, music on144–145, dialogue on147–148

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Different routes into women's public leadership
claimBlocks.text: Aguirre Pérez's 2004 study follows three Xochistlahuaca women—Florentina López de Jesús, Josefina Flores and Martha Sánchez Néstor—to examine differing routes into public leadership. Interviews connect participation with education, paid work, family position and organizing. The author also identifies barriers inside parties and local institutions, including heavy workloads and unequal access to information. These selected life histories show differences among women's experiences; they are not a current portrait of every Amuzgo community.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A project's own statement of purpose
claimBlocks.text: Radio Ñomndaa's April 2013 statement presents the station as an Indigenous community medium independent of government, parties and religious organizations. It connects communication with strengthening culture, sharing information and respecting other peoples. This primary statement records the project's stated purposes. It should be read alongside more substantial research, without treating an old schedule as proof of current service or assigning the project's political commitments to every Amuzgo person.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Direct post, dated April11,2013; mission paragraph

identityAndGeographyNotes: These actual readings primarily concern Xochistlahuaca/Suljaa’ in Guerrero. They cannot substitute for San Pedro Amuzgos or Santa María Ipalapa community histories in Oaxaca.
Nn’anncue Ñomndaa is retained as the self-designation used by the Guerrero author/project; no claim that every town uses the same spelling or language variety.

A civil association, school project, community radio, municipal authority and people are different subjects. The radio and its account of autonomy are not a single government for every Amuzgo community.
Mobility in Aguirre's life-history research is dated and individual; no current migration rate, destination count or community-wide demographic claim is proposed.

researchGaps: An accessible original monograph or direct historical land archive would strengthen nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century coverage; indexed snippets were not promoted to evidence.
Oaxaca communities need distinct public community histories and institutions, rather than projection of Xochistlahuaca examples across the state border.
The sources provide dated participant accounts and scholarly interpretations, not present-day officeholder lists, measured educational outcomes, current radio operations or legal advice.
Additional public Amuzgo-authored histories, particularly women and migrant community accounts, could broaden voices without inventing a consensus.
